Federal prosecutors have uncovered an alleged cargo theft conspiracy involving at least 24 freight shipments and millions in stolen merchandise. Investigators say suspects took control of established trucking companies and used their identities to secure legitimate freight contracts. Drivers then collected shipments from distribution facilities, but the cargo never reached its intended destinations. Authorities estimate that thefts involving one defendant exceeded $12 million in retail value.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut announced federal charges against Nursulton Khaydarov on October 21. Khaydarov, 33, is a citizen of Uzbekistan and lawful permanent resident of the United States. Prosecutors accuse him of participating in a conspiracy that targeted interstate shipments from California and other locations. He pleaded not guilty during an appearance in federal court in Bridgeport, Connecticut.
According to federal investigators, the operation began around September 2025 and involved multiple motor carriers. Participants purchased trucking businesses or otherwise assumed control of their existing operations. They obtained U.S. Department of Transportation numbers, motor carrier identification numbers, business email accounts and ownership identities. The group then impersonated previous owners to negotiate transportation agreements with freight brokers.
How the alleged carrier takeover scheme worked
The suspects relied on established business identities rather than creating entirely new trucking companies. Prosecutors contend that these arrangements allowed participants to exploit existing reputations and relationships within the freight industry. Brokers negotiated interstate transportation contracts with individuals posing as legitimate carrier representatives. After drivers collected the merchandise, the shipments disappeared before reaching their scheduled delivery locations.
The scheme resembles a growing problem involving the buying and selling of established trucking companies. Some operators acquire existing businesses to obtain operating histories, established credentials and relationships with freight brokers. Older authorities may pass routine vetting more easily because their federal records already show years of activity. FMCSA has warned against buying, selling or leasing operating authority outside legitimate corporate transactions.
For freight brokers, the challenge extends beyond confirming an active DOT number or valid insurance. Recent ownership changes, updated contact information and unfamiliar email domains can warrant additional verification. Insurance changes and inconsistencies between registration records also deserve closer examination. An established operating history means little if brokers cannot verify who actually controls the company.
The indictment describes additional steps participants allegedly took to conceal their activities. Prosecutors accuse the group of switching tractor license plates and using burner phones with encrypted messaging applications. Court records also describe efforts to defeat electronic shipment tracking systems. Investigators contend that participants provided false explanations about delayed or missing freight after completing pickups.
Images from an FBI affidavit show a tractor-trailer and a close-up of its license plate, which investigators examined during an alleged $12 million cargo theft conspiracy. (Source: FBI affidavit/U.S. District Court)
Federal investigators also documented ransom demands involving stolen shipments. According to the indictment, participants requested cryptocurrency or electronic transfers in exchange for returning merchandise. An FBI affidavit identifies approximately $121,000 in cryptocurrency that Khaydarov’s Coinbase account received across 33 transactions. Those payments occurred between November 2025 and May 2026, although investigators did not establish that every transfer represented ransom.
The stolen merchandise covered several categories of commercial freight. Prosecutors identified hard drives, stereo equipment, clothing, electronics and computer equipment among the missing products. Other shipments contained food items, nicotine products and additional consumer goods. Investigators attributed more than $12 million in estimated retail losses to thefts involving Khaydarov personally.
Multiple driver identities uncovered
Federal court documents also describe several fraudulent driver’s licenses connected to Khaydarov. Authorities identified five different names appearing on those documents. Each license displayed his photograph with altered facial features. Investigators also confirmed that he possessed a valid New Jersey commercial driver’s license.
A photograph included in an FBI affidavit shows an individual investigators identify as Nursulton Khaydarov inside a truck cab during the cargo theft investigation. (Source: FBI affidavit/U.S. District Court)
One documented incident involved a pistachio shipment departing Terra Bella, California, for Laredo, Texas, on December 19, 2025. Investigators reported that the driver presented an Illinois license identifying him as Sayid Makhmudarov. State motor vehicle records showed no matching license, and photographs connected that document to Khaydarov. California’s pistachio industry has faced growing concerns over cargo theft , particularly during harvest season when high-value shipments enter transportation networks.
On May 18, police in Ontario, California, located a tractor-trailer associated with suspected cargo thefts. During a traffic stop, Khaydarov identified himself using his valid New Jersey driver’s license. Officers discovered suspected counterfeit identification and a nicotine product matching merchandise from an earlier theft. Police impounded the equipment, and FBI agents subsequently searched the tractor under a federal warrant.
A tractor-trailer that federal investigators linked to an alleged cargo theft conspiracy involving at least 24 shipments and more than $12 million in stolen merchandise. (Photo: FBI affidavit/U.S. District Court)
Federal authorities arrested Khaydarov in Ontario, California, on June 1, 2026, following a criminal complaint. A grand jury in New Haven, Connecticut, returned an indictment on September 22. The indictment charges him with conspiracy, which carries a maximum prison sentence of five years. He has remained in custody since his arrest.
Federal investigation continues across multiple agencies
The FBI leads the investigation with assistance from several federal and local enforcement partners. Participating agencies include Homeland Security Investigations, IRS Criminal Investigation and the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General. Police departments in Fullerton and Ontario, California, also contributed investigative resources. Assistant U.S. Attorneys David T. Huang and Larysa J. Kern are handling the prosecution.
U.S. Attorney David X. Sullivan and FBI Special Agent in Charge P.J. O’Brien announced the charges. Khaydarov has pleaded not guilty, and the charges are allegations. Investigators have not publicly identified the affected carriers, brokers, shippers or distribution facilities. Authorities also have not disclosed how participants acquired control of the trucking businesses.
The announcement leaves the recovery status of the stolen merchandise unresolved. Anyone with relevant information can contact the FBI’s New Haven Field Office at 203-777-6311.
Why It Matters
This case shows how criminals can exploit established carrier identities to obtain freight through legitimate brokerage transactions. Existing DOT numbers, operating histories and business email accounts cannot independently establish who controls a transportation company.
CFCO
In my opinion, this case reinforces why verification must go beyond an active DOT number. The Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) course teaches a five-layer process to identify inconsistencies before freight changes hands. Technology helps, but trained employees must know what to question and when to stop.

Kia is betting its new lineup of affordable EVs, like the EV3 , can beat the incoming wave of Chinese models in Canada, but affordability is only one part of the equation.
Kia bets on affordable EVs to take on China in Canada
After launching the EV3 in Canada in August, Kia said it was the lowest-priced electric vehicle on the market, starting at CAD $39,744.
It may not hold the title for long, though. Canada struck a deal with China earlier this year, allowing up to 49,000 electric vehicles to enter the Canadian market at a 6.1% tariff rate.

SONAR has released three new truckload dataset groups that measure what shippers pay their transportation providers — brokers and carriers — as freight moves through a routing guide and as contract rates reset. SONAR also expanded SearchCarriers with carrier watchlists, email alerts, inspection search and equipment lookup by VIN or license plate.
The new data answers a question shippers have long had to estimate on their own: how much more does a load cost when the primary carrier says no?
Key takeaways
Routing Guide Premium (RGP2.USA, RGP3.USA) shows the median percentage change in the all-in cost a shipper pays its provider when a load is accepted on the second or third tender instead of the first.
Routing Guide Acceptance Share (RGAS1.USA, RGAS2.USA, RGAS3.USA) shows what share of accepted loads is accepted at each tender position, from first tender through fifth and beyond.
Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA) shows the average percentage change between new and previous contract base rates, signaling where contract pricing — and bid pressure — is heading.
All three dataset groups update daily on a 7-day rolling average.
SearchCarriers now supports up to 200 carrier watches per user, email notifications, inspection search and equipment lookup by VIN or plate.
New datasets: routing guide performance and contract rate trends
All three new dataset groups measure shipper-to-provider costs — the rates shippers pay to the brokers and carriers that move their freight. They are not carrier operating costs or broker margins.
Each dataset updates daily using a 7-day rolling average and is available now in SONAR.
Routing Guide Premium (RGP2.USA, RGP3.USA)
Routing Guide Premium measures the median percentage increase or decrease in all-in transportation costs — base rate, fuel and accessorial charges — that a shipper pays its provider on a later tender compared with the initial tender.
RGP2.USA: premium paid when a load is accepted on the second tender vs. the first
RGP3.USA: premium paid when a load is accepted on the third tender vs. the first
Why it matters: it puts a dollar-based percentage on routing guide failure, so shippers can see the true cost of freight slipping past their primary provider
As of Oct. 20, 2026, loads accepted on the second tender cost shippers a median 22.02% more all-in than first-tender loads. Third-tender loads cost 26.44% more. Both premiums spiked above 30% around the December holidays, early February and late June into July.
Routing Guide Premium (RGP2.USA, RGP3.USA) and Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA), Oct. 2025–Oct. 2026. Source: SONAR.
Routing Guide Acceptance Share measures the percentage of accepted loads at each tender position , from the first tender through the fifth and beyond.
RGAS1.USA: share of loads accepted on the first tender
RGAS2.USA / RGAS3.USA: share accepted on the second and third tenders
Why it matters: it shows how efficiently routing guides are performing and how often freight falls to backup providers — where the premiums above apply
As of Oct. 20, 2026, 89.05% of accepted loads were accepted on the first tender, below the 12-month average of 91.60%. Second-tender acceptances made up 6.84% and third-tender 4.11% .
Routing Guide Acceptance Share by tender position (RGAS1.USA, RGAS2.USA, RGAS3.USA). Source: SONAR.
Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA)
Contract Rate Change Direction measures the average percentage change between new and previous contract base rates that shippers pay providers. It only counts changes where the prior contract rate was stable for more than 90 days, filtering out short-term noise.
Positive values: new contract rates are resetting higher than the rates they replace
Why it matters: it helps shippers, brokers and carriers spot contract pricing trends and potential bid timing pressure
As of Oct. 20, 2026, CRCD.USA stood at 12.58% , meaning new contract base rates averaged about 12.6% above the rates they replaced. That is well above the 12-month average of 8.34%, and the index has climbed steadily since late 2025 (see chart above).
How the three datasets work together
Dataset | Tickers | Question it answers
Routing Guide Premium | RGP2.USA, RGP3.USA | How much more do I pay my provider when freight moves past the first tender?
Routing Guide Acceptance Share | RGAS1.USA, RGAS2.USA, RGAS3.USA | How often does freight move past the first tender?
Contract Rate Change Direction | CRCD.USA | Are new contract rates resetting higher or lower than the old ones?
Combined, they show both how often a routing guide breaks and what it costs when it does — the core inputs for deciding when to rebid.
SearchCarriers: expanded carrier monitoring and qualification tools
SearchCarriers now does more than a one-time carrier check. New monitoring and search tools let brokers and shippers keep watching a carrier after onboarding and pull safety and equipment details in seconds.
Carrier watchlists
Add carriers to a personal Company Watches list by company name or USDOT number
Track up to 200 carriers per user, or add many at once with Bulk Import
Choose what to monitor for each carrier: inspections, contact info, reported trucks, reported trailers, reported drivers, MCS-150 overdue status, for-sale monitoring and out-of-service orders — or select All updates
SearchCarriers Company Watches: monitor carriers by USDOT number and pick the changes that trigger alerts. Source: SONAR SearchCarriers.
Email notifications
Get an email when a watched carrier changes, based on the alert types you selected
Add and verify a notification email in settings to turn alerts on
Why it matters: changes such as a new out-of-service order, updated contact details or an overdue MCS-150 can signal risk or possible fraud — and now reach your inbox instead of waiting for the next manual check
Inspection search
Search for a specific carrier inspection to pull up its details quickly
Supports faster safety and compliance reviews during qualification and audits
Equipment lookup by VIN or license plate
Search by VIN or license plate to see available information on a truck or trailer
Helps confirm that the equipment showing up at the dock matches the carrier you booked
What this means for carrier qualification
Carrier qualification no longer ends at onboarding. With watchlists, alerts, inspection search and equipment lookup, teams can:
Monitor continuously rather than re-vetting carriers by hand
Catch red flags earlier , such as out-of-service orders or contact changes
Verify equipment against the carrier of record before freight is loaded
Reach safety and compliance data faster during audits and claims
Frequently asked questions
What is a routing guide premium? A routing guide premium is the extra all-in cost a shipper pays its broker or carrier when a load is accepted on a backup tender instead of the first tender. SONAR’s RGP2.USA and RGP3.USA measure the median premium for second- and third-tender loads, including base rate , fuel and accessorials.
Do the new SONAR datasets show carrier costs or shipper costs? They show shipper-to-provider costs: the rates shippers pay brokers and carriers. They do not measure carrier operating costs or broker margins.
What is routing guide acceptance share? Routing guide acceptance share is the percentage of accepted loads at each tender position. SONAR’s RGAS1.USA tracks the first tender, with RGAS2.USA and RGAS3.USA tracking the second and third tenders.
How does SONAR measure contract rate changes? CRCD.USA measures the average percentage change between new and previous contract base rates. It only counts changes where the prior contract rate was stable for more than 90 days.
How often do the new datasets update? All three dataset groups update daily using a 7-day rolling average.
How does SearchCarriers help with carrier qualification? SearchCarriers lets users watch up to 200 carriers, get email alerts on changes like out-of-service orders or overdue MCS-150 filings, search specific inspections, and look up equipment by VIN or license plate.
See the new data in SONAR
Routing Guide Premium, Routing Guide Acceptance Share and Contract Rate Change Direction are live in SONAR today, alongside the expanded SearchCarriers tools.
Request a SONAR demo to see what your freight costs when it moves past the first tender.

The CGI Kingdom Just Put New Wheels on the Tesla Roadster, Does It Change Anything?
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | Vossen
It’s been a little over a week since the new-generation Tesla Roadster was demonstrated. We would have said fully unveiled, but it was nothing more than a demonstration that split petrolheads opinions, as while some think its party tricks will make it to the production version, others call it fake using more words.
Now, the model may have been demonstrated, and back then, it took social media by storm. It instantly became viral, and everyone and their pet spoke about it, regardless of whether they are into cars or not. Like every viral thing, most people and companies wanted a piece of the action, hence the numerous AI-generated videos that have hit the World Wide Web since, joined by the usual memes, and quite a few renderings that are on the more realistic side of things.
In this case, we do not have a pixel master to thank for these digital illustrations, as they came directly from Vossen’s social media channels. The wheelmaker saw the opportunity and decided to imagine what the new Tesla Roadster would look like on one of their alloy sets. Thus, they set to work, and came up with the CGIs that you can see in the gallery above, which, at first glance, do not seem like computer generated images whatsoever.
But that is what they are, because no one can get their hands on this model, no matter how loaded and well-connected they may be, because it doesn’t exist yet. It should enter production in 2028. That’s what Elon Musk claims, but then again, he said that this thing will be on the roads in 2020, three years after the concept broke cover. Then he said that it will hit the assembly line in 2021, 2022, and 2023, as well as “hopefully” in 2024, so you can understand my skepticism.
Photo: Instagram | Vossen Thus, it may not be ready yet, though it still managed to go viral due to its ability to jump and break its fall, because it has thrusters, in case you forgot. There are 10 cold-gas thrusters fed by ultra-high-pressure air from a pair of 600-liter tanks that are on deck, and it is these thrusters that allow it to hit 60 mph (97 kph) in less than 1 second. The time is 0.81 seconds, officially, according to Tesla . The fans underneath provide 2Gs of downforce while the vehicle stands still.
And it is due to these that the new Tesla Roadster can pull some very impressive stunts. Mind you, it’s not a flying car per se, as it is more of a jumping one, and as mentioned above, it can break its fall using the thrusters. On paper, anyway, and on the demonstrated vehicle, because in real life, we reckon it will be a huge hassle to make it work and make it safe for reasons that have already been discussed multiple times.
Now, since we know what the Tesla Roadste r is capable of, and that it does not look like the concept anymore, but like a mix between the Cybertruck and a supercar from a few years ago, let’s move on to the Vossen-related reason behind this story, namely the wheels that equip the rendered vehicle.
These have a disc-like pattern, are a bit concave from what we can see, and slightly larger than the OEM ones equipping the the tester that was demonstrated a few days ago. They sport a silver look, just like the rest of the car, and if you were wondering what they are called, then the answer comes from Vossen, and it is the LC3-11T.
Photo: Instagram | Vossen The alloys are not exactly brand new, as they have been around for a few years now. The company’s official website reveals that these are available in multiple sizes, from 19 to 24 inches in diameter, joined by a 26-inch proposal. Pricing for the smallest set starts at $10,400, whereas the 24-inch set kicks off at $12,400, and for the 26-inch one, you are looking at a minimum of $13,200.
Mind you, these prices exclude any options that you may be interested in, as well as the tires, so the alloys in question are not exactly on the affordable side of things. One can choose between the 48 custom finishes available, including the Gloss Clear look of the pictured set. And if you are wondering what other rides sit on Vossen’s LC3-11T, then the answer is the Mercedes S-Class, EQS, G-Wagen, Range Rover, Bentley Continental GT, BMW 7 Series, and others, according to the wheelmaker’s official website.
Now, I’m not exactly a fan of the new Roadster , nor any other Tesla out there, and the same goes for the entire EV crowd, regardless of the make and model, but to me, this machine looks better than the stock one when riding on these new alloys. Still, due to the extreme engineering that has gone into the model, chances are it won’t be a walk in the park to fit new wheels to it. I Tested Some New Gran Turismo 7 Engine Swaps to Warm Up for the Latest Time Trial
17 photos
Photo: autoevolution
It’s raining outside and I’m just itching to jump in the RX-8 and go “buy some bread”. I just know I won’t be able to behave if I do so, especially since I was so chill about driving for nine hours straight yesterday. At least it’s Thursday and I can log in to Gran Turismo 7 for the new Time Trial.
Sometimes I think that I may be so obsessed with racing because of all the video games I played in the late ‘90s and early 2000s.
But then again, spending years and years with Real Time Strategy titles and shooters didn’t make me want to join the army or anything along those lines.
And I know I will often say the virtual world is no match for the real world, which is still 100% valid. While I’m working on starting my own real race team, spending more time in front of a TV screen is currently my only option.
And I just knew I could get a fast lap at Barcelona-Catalunya (GP Layout, no chicane), as I must have racked up thousands of laps around it in 25+ years. By the way, I’m still trying to raise enough credits for a McLaren F1. Even though I scored 250K from the Fugu Z Time Trial plus the two Stealth Cars from the Viewers Campaign, I’m not quite there yet.
Honda-Swapped Citroën 2 CV 6 Charleston '86 Photo: autoevolution Nine times out of ten, I will tell you that it’s simply not worth doing engine swaps in Gran Turismo 7. But ever since Spec IV arrived, I’ve been thinking about checking out the latest ones. I initially upgraded the Citroen 2 CV 6 Charleston for a Weekly Challenge event, and found out it could handle the extra power.
Going for a Honda Integra Type R B18C engine will turn the heat up a little more, and it’s not particularly expensive either. You’ll also gain a few pounds while you’re at it, but the whole package will still weigh less than two Honda Goldwing motorcycles put together.
If you know how much I like Hondas, you’ll realize why I had no choice but to go for a Spoon livery. I was surprised to get wheelspin in fourth gear, and annoyed to discover I had forgotten that’s as far as this gearbox will go.
A top speed of 113 mph/182 kph is anything but ideal for a track like Barcelona-Catalunya, where the main straight is over 0.62 miles/1,000 meters long. Anyway, the Citroen/Honda hybrid felt strange to drive, but decently fast nonetheless. Being that light it almost doesn’t need to slow down for the corners ahead, and I scored a 2:03.370 on my second lap.
Ferrari F355 Berlinetta '94 Race Car Photo: autoevolution Have you seen the latest upgrade on the Ferrari 12Cilindri? YouTube was buzzing with videos on the topic, and Jason Camissa’s take on the whole thing was my favorite.
Who would’ve thought people would be happy to get a simulated manual gearbox on a Ferrari in 2026? When the F355 F1 showed up, I just knew I had to go back to GT7 and drive my virtual one again. I thought I’d bring it up to GT4 spec by increasing the power output and lowering the weight, but I may have gone overboard with the whole thing (418 bhp/2,678 lbs/1,215 kg).
After installing a widebodykit (100,000 credits), I looked at some of the 24 pages filled with custom liveries and opted for the Momo theme (42,500 more credits). Shouldn’t people get paid for the liveries they make for this game ?
Or is that a thing and I’m just not aware of it? Anyway, I found myself hitting 161 mph/260 kph just before Turn 1, thinking I might aim for a GT3 spec next. Despite the RH tires, I still went sideways a few times, especially in the second, right hand corner. My fastest lap was a 1:52.176, and I had a feeling I’d improve in the Honda Step WGN.
V12 Powered Honda Step WGN Spada Premium Line '23 Photo: autoevolution It obviously wasn’t going to happen with the stock setup, even after going for all the upgrades. There are three engine swap choices for this machine, and you can easily build a Renault Espace F1 opponent if you don’t mind spending 600,000 credits.
That’s right, that’s how much you’ll be spending for the F3500-A engine, which will get you an increase of over 600 horsepower and a boatload of torque. Combine that with some RS tires and all the weight reduction packages, and you’ve got yourself an insane build.
I was almost certain I could lap Barcelona in 1:45, and it did! The gearing is something to get used to, as this car will do 80 mph/130 kph in first.
I was doing nearly 186 mph/300 kph before the first corner, and it’s all quite manageable if you ask me. The sad part was knowing the car for the Time Trial wouldn’t be nearly as fast.
Time Trial Photo: autoevolution That’s right, I already knew the Hyundai Elantra N TC ‘24 would be no match for the V12-powered wagon. Just two and a half hours after the event went live, Calster was the fastest in the world with a 1:50.281. The target for Gold was 1:53.589, while the one for Bronze was 2:01.309.
I already had a Sprite-themed version of the car, and was somewhat annoyed to see the BoP rules come into play again. That means you get access to less power while having to deal with more weight.
I improved to 1:54.610 after just three laps, and that should be good enough for the Silver Record Reward. Tidgney mentioned it should be easy to go even faster than that, which is why I recommend watching his tutorial on the fast lap bellow.
I preferred seeing what my GT500-spec NSX was capable of, and the 1:40.821 I scored is one of my fastest laps around this track ever. I’ll be back with more information on the Weekly Challenges soon!

Russian YouTubers Build Quad Combustion-Engined AWD Car, Each Wheel Has Its Own Power and Gearbox
44 photos
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54
The most wide-spread internal combustion engine architecture of today is the four-cylinder version, for may substantiated reason that meet several requirements imposed by distinct sectors, from financial to engineering to marketing to production. Typically, the four cylinders happily coexist within a single block, reciprocating in tandem and working in harmony to make a car move. But what if they didn’t?
If IT's stupid but it works, don't fix IT. IT ain't stupid, you just don't get IT. Four engines in a four-wheeled automobile are perfectly reasonable. I mean, if a wheel is designed to turn, why should it only be a passive participant to the ride, instead of doing some work? Oh, right, there that AWD thing. But that means four wheels share one engine. That’s not independence, is it? Garage 54 has a solution for this.
You probably remember the Russians from Novosibirsk (that’s in Siberia, in the middle of the biggest country of Earth), that constantly challenge everything the automotive universe holds dear. They don’t mean any harm. They just do it because it’s fun. And sometimes, simply because “If you could, you should.”
Garage 54 is never tired of finding new automotive limits to break. This time, they didn't have to venture to frontiers no one has gone before. Quite frankly, they didn't have to dig for inspiration, too. After all, we've all heard about multi-motor EVs, right? Well, why can't internal combustion have poly-engined representatives?
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54 Vladislav Barashenkov and his fearless crew of Siberian wrenching gremlins looked at modern quad-motor electric hypercars and decided that silent, computer-controlled torque vectoring is for cowards. Why let microchips and copper windings have all the fun when you can cram four separate gasoline engines into one car?
It is a glorious monument to mechanical overcomplication, built on the unshakable philosophy that four tiny, uncoordinated pistons beat one sensible, cohesive, time-tested drivetrain.
To turn this fever dream into reality, the team bypassed exotic racing crate motors and bought the cheapest powerplants on the Russian market for 32,500 rubles (or about $340) apiece. Spending 130,000 rubles in total, they acquired four Chinese-built 150-cc single-cylinder, four-stroke, air-cooled engines based on the ubiquitous GY6 utility architecture. Normally, these humble units are designed to propel lightweight quad bikes, small agricultural trikes, and budget recreational dune buggies.
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54 What these miniature powerhouses lack in prestige, they make up for in sheer packaging convenience. Each 150-cc unit churns out a pavement-wrinkling 10 horsepower, giving the four-engine automobile a theoretical combined output of 40 horsepower. Better yet, every motor comes factory-equipped with an electric starter, a continuously variable transmission, an integrated differential, and a reverse gearbox, meaning this Franken-car can theoretically creep forward and backward just like that.
Every crime against automotive engineering requires a willing victim, and the crew selected their battle-scarred Toyota Aristo—also known as a first-generation Lexus GS—which had already endured numerous engine-swap experiments. Because the executive sedan left the factory as a rear-wheel-drive machine, its front wheel hubs lacked drive splines.
Worse still, routing half-shafts toward the front 15-inch wheels meant colliding directly with the shock struts, control arms, and original factory steering linkages.
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54 Rather than surrendering to basic geometry, or automotive common sense, the mechanics decided to tear out the entire front suspension and convert the luxury sedan to all-wheel drive the hard way. After briefly considering components from a front-wheel-drive Lada Samara, they settled on transplanting the front subframe and suspension from a rugged Lada Niva 4x4.
This unholy Japanese-Russian marriage consumed two weeks of non-stop cutting, grinding, and heavy structural welding inside the Siberian workshop. Plus a heavy dose of Russian optimism, which can be best resumed to this generic idea “It probably won’t work as planned, so let’s do it anyway.”
Fitting a narrow Lada Niva crossmember beneath the wide body of a Lexus required fabrication techniques that would make a structural engineer weep. Instead of gutting the thick factory frame rails completely, the crew grafted sections of Niva frame rails directly into the chassis and fabricated custom upper spring towers. They then sliced the Niva crossmember in half, widened it to match the track, and bridged the gap with steel pipe.
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54 With the suspension cobbled together, shoehorning the four powerplants into the car took another full week of trial and error. Because the two front engines were too wide to sit side by side, one motor had to be mounted slightly higher than its neighbor. Rather than using direct shafts, the builders linked each engine to its corresponding CV axle via exposed roller chains, steel sprockets, and custom-welded shaft sleeves. Safety is for weaklings in Russia, and Garage 54 doesn’t believe in all this New Age fad.
An initial spin test on the workshop lift revealed craftsmanship that could generously be described as artisanal. As the front wheels turned under power, the engines wobbled on their mounts, the chains rattled angrily, and one sprocket rotated with a noticeably square eccentricity. While the massive gear reduction promised brisk low-speed torque rather than highway velocity, the mechanics openly debated whether the spliced axles or suspension would snap in half first.
Out back, the fabricators carved away chunks of rusty sheet metal—carefully sparing the last shreds of chassis reinforcement—to stuff the remaining two engines over the rear axle. Synchronizing this mechanical quartet required one full day just to rig four separate Bowden cables to a single gas pedal. At one point, the car casually began smoking rather vigorously while the welder worked inside, a minor inconvenience the crew greeted with peak Siberian nonchalance.
Photo: YouTube/Garage 54 Physics delivered its first reality check the moment the sedan was lowered off the lift onto its wheels. As the suspension compressed under the vehicle's weight, the axle geometry shifted, turning the carefully calculated chain tension into slack metal spaghetti and tilting the front mounts at alarming angles.
Firing up all four engines produced a glorious, buzzsaw symphony of 600-cc fury as the sedan lurched out of the garage at full 107% percent capacity. Almost immediately, a bracket weld snapped and a chain jumped its misaligned sprocket, trimming propulsion to 75 percent. Unbothered by the carnage, Barashenkov pressed on as two more chains derailed, systematically cutting output to 50 percent and finally 25 percent of total available power.
Herein lies the accidental genius of this absurd multi-engine architecture: ultimate mechanical redundancy. Even after three drive chains had surrendered their will to live, that final 10-horsepower engine faithfully pulled the heavy sedan forward, shifted into reverse, and drove the car back into the shop.
It is a chaotic, chain-snapping triumph that proves poly-engined combustion actually works (efficiency not withstanding). Once the Garage 54 band of wrenching rebels finds a way to devise a sound plan and stick to it, electric vehicles should officially have a mighty 40-horsepower reason to be terrified.
